You will think about why we consume the way we do, and what it costs us and the world around us. Through four lessons, you will read, listen, discuss, and write about consumption and start to think more carefully about your own habits as a consumer. SECTION A : Food Awareness 4 ١ 1 Do you think people waste more food today than in the past? Food Waste Every year, a large amount of food is wasted around the world. This is because people buy more than they need, store food poorly, and misunderstand food labels. Food waste increases in houses, supermarkets, and during special times and festivals. However, simple actions such as better habits and awareness can help reduce this problem. Inquiry Question: ٠ Where do you think most food waste happens: at home, at shops, or on farms? What do you think is the biggest reason for food waste in Egypt? Discussion in groups of four: Explain ٠ How does our perception of food safety influence the amount of food we discard? Formal Report The Causes of Food Waste in Egyptian Homes Introduction: This report looks at the main reasons why food is wasted in Egyptian homes. It uses information from consumer surveys and local studies. The results show that food waste in Egypt is a serious problem that needs to be addressed. Project: What do you think the writer will say next about food waste? 105 Unit 4 : The Power of Choice

JRE (Justify - Reason - Evidence) 1. Is food waste more of an individual problem or a social problem? - Use evidence from the report to support your answer. 2. To what extent could the proposed recommendations shift the culture of food waste in Egypt? Justify. 106 Findings (Causes): In Egypt, one common cause of food waste is buying more food than a family can use. During Ramadan, some families may prepare or purchase a large amount of food to welcome guests and express generosity. Although generosity is a positive and valued tradition, poor planning can sometimes lead to more food being prepared than needed. As a result, some of the extra food may be wasted. A second important cause is storing food incorrectly. Many homes do not have good refrigerators or dry storage. As a result, fresh food — especially bread, fruit, and vegetables — goes bad faster than it should. Bread waste alone is a major issue in Egypt. A third cause is confusion about dates on food packages. Many people throw away food on or before its “best before’ date. However, ‘best before’ only means that the taste or quality might change — it does not mean the food is unsafe. The ‘use by’ date is the one that tells you when food is no longer safe to eat. Discuss: Which cause of food waste seems most common in your community? Recommendations: Based on these findings, this report suggests three actions. First, schools should teach students about food shopping and storage from an early age. Second, shops should be required to give safe leftover food to food banks rather than throw it away. Third, food labels should be made clearer so that people understand the difference between “best before’ and ‘use by’. Evaluate: Which recommendation would have the biggest impact? Why? Conclusion: The evidence shows that most food waste in Egypt can be reduced through education and better habits. These changes do not cost a lot of money. If these recommendations are followed, the amount of food waste in Egyptian homes could go down significantly within a few years. Concept 4: Consumption and Choice

¢ Oral Review Presentation: Task: Prepare and deliver a 2-minute spoken review of a digital platform or app of your choice. To succeed, follow these steps: 1. Choose your topic: Select a digital platform or app that you know well and have a clear opinion about. 2. Identify your audience: Consider who you are speaking to (e.g. classmates, potential users). 3. Plan your structure: Your review must follow the same four-part structure as the written review. 4. Prepare your notes: You may use brief notes (maximum 5). 5. Practice: Do not read from a full script. Speak naturally to engage your audience. Structure of a Review ¢ A well-written review follows a clear four-part structure. Each paragraph has a specific purpose. Part Purpose What to Include Paragraph 1 | Introduction | Name the subject of the review. Give essential background information. State your overall impression in one sentence. Paragraph 2 | Positives Describe the strengths of the subject. Use specific examples or evidence. Explain why each point is positive. Discuss the weaknesses or limitations fairly. Avoid being overly tough. Use a balanced, simple and professional tone. Paragraph 3 | Negatives Paragraph 4 | Conclusion | Summarize your overall judgement. State who you would recommend it to, and why. End with a memorable final sentence. A review is a critical evaluation of a subject — such as a book, product, service, performance, or piece of writing. Its primary purpose is to provide an informed opinion that helps others decide whether they should engage with that subject or avoid it. 121 Unit 4 : The Power of Choice

4.4 The Psychology of the Sale: Why We Buy What We Do Not Need Sale events make people feel excited and believe they are saving money! However, companies use clever tricks to influence our decisions and push us to buy more. These tricks create urgency and make products seem more valuable than they really are. In the end, many people spend more than they planned, even when they think they are saving. ٠ The word “falling for’’ in the text is closest in meaning to : a. avoiding b. being tricked by c. understanding d. comparing Every year, millions of people around the world wait for events like Black Friday to go shopping. They feel excited as they plan their purchases in advance and believe they are making smart choices. But are they really saving money, or are they falling for a set of very clever tricks? ٠ What happens to the jacket price in the example? One of the most common tricks is called loss aversion. Imagine a jacket that costs 400 Egyptian pounds. You do not really need it. Then a sign appears: “Was 800 LE, Now 400 LE, Save 50%!’ Suddenly, the jacket feels much more attractive. Your brain tells you, ‘If I don’t buy it, I will lose the chance to save 400 pounds.’ Of course, you have not lost anything, but that is how our brains work. Not buying something feels like a loss. ٠ Name two tricks used in sales. Sale events also use other tricks. Phrases like ‘Only 3 left in stock!’ create a feeling of urgency. You feel that you must decide immediately or you will miss the chance. When you see many other people buying something, you think it must be a good idea. And countdown clocks on websites force you to decide quickly, before you have time to think carefully. All three tricks work together to push you towards buying. ٠ Do you think people really save money during sales? Why or why not? Research has found something surprising: people who shop during sales actually spend more money overall than people who do not. They feel they have saved money, but in fact they have spent more. The sale is not designed to save you money. It is designed to make you spend more and feel happy about it. 124 Concept 4: Consumption and Choice

&) Read the text, then answer the questions. When Places Remember A historical landscape is more than a collection of old buildings, monuments, and ruins. It is a place where events from the past have left visible or invisible traces. A battlefield, an ancient street, a former factory, or even an ordinary house can become a site of memory when people connect it with important events, experiences, or individuals. Such places help communities remember their past and consider how it continues to influence the present. However, sites of memory do not tell their stories automatically. The meaning of a place often depends on how it is preserved and presented. A ruined building, for example, may appear meaningless to a visitor who knows nothing about its history. Signs, photographs, recorded memories, and personal objects can provide context and transform a visit to an unfamiliar place into a powerful historical experience. In this way, interpretation becomes as important as preservation. This means that museums act as storytellers, but storytelling also involves responsibility. Museums must decide whose experiences to include and which voices may have been ignored in the past. Traditional exhibitions often focused on powerful leaders and major political events. Today, many museums also include the experiences of workers, women, children, minority communities, and ordinary families. By presenting different perspectives, museums can offer a more complex understanding of history. Technology has also changed how historical stories are communicated. Interactive screens, digital reconstructions, audio recordings, and virtual reality can help visitors imagine places that no longer exist or events that no longer occur. Nevertheless, technology should support the historical story rather than distract from it. Impressive digital effects are of little value if visitors leave without understanding why a place or object matters. Ultimately, historical landscapes and museums connect memory with the present. They remind us that history is not simply a list of dates and events. It consists of human experiences that can be remembered, interpreted, and sometimes debated. By preserving significant places and telling their stories carefully, societies can help future generations understand both where they came from and how the past continues to shape their world. A.
